title: What Ofsted Inspectors Actually Ask Frontline Staff
meta_description: Realistic questions Ofsted inspectors ask residential childcare staff during inspection, and principles for answering honestly, confidently and well.
summary: Ofsted inspectors routinely speak to frontline staff during children's home inspections, and those conversations carry real weight. This guide sets out the questions staff are most often asked, what inspectors are listening for, and how to answer honestly without rehearsed scripts.
key_legislation: Social care common inspection framework (SCCIF) for children's homes
Working Together to Safeguard Children (statutory guidance)
body_html:
Under the social care common inspection framework (SCCIF), Ofsted inspectors spend most of an inspection gathering first-hand evidence: talking to children, observing daily life, reading records, and talking to staff at every level. If you work in a children's home, an inspector will at some point sit down with you, often informally, in the kitchen or during an activity, and ask questions. This is not a trap and it is not a memory test. Inspectors are trying to find out whether what the paperwork says is what actually happens, and whether staff know the children well enough to keep them safe and help them progress.

What inspectors are really assessing

SCCIF judgements centre on the experiences and progress of children, how well they are helped and protected, and the effectiveness of leaders and managers. When an inspector talks to you, they are triangulating: does what this staff member says match the care plans, the incident records, what children told me, and what I have seen on shift? Consistency between those sources is the strongest evidence a home can offer. Inconsistency, such as staff who cannot describe a child's risks, or who describe a sanctions culture the paperwork hides, is what sinks judgements.

Questions you can realistically expect

About the children

  • Tell me about the children living here. What are they each like?
  • What progress has this child made since they arrived? How do you know?
  • What are this child's main risks, and what is in place to manage them?
  • What does this child's care plan say you are working on with them?
  • How do you support this child's education and health appointments?

About safeguarding

  • What would you do if a child told you a member of staff had hurt them?
  • What is your procedure when a child goes missing? What happens when they come back?
  • What do you know about criminal and sexual exploitation risks for these children?
  • Who is your designated safeguarding lead, and how do you contact the local authority designated officer (LADO)?
  • Have you ever raised a concern? What happened?

About whistleblowing and culture

  • What would you do if you had concerns about your manager?
  • Do you know how to contact Ofsted directly?
  • Would you feel safe raising concerns here? Why?

About you and the home

  • How long have you worked here? What was your induction like?
  • When was your last supervision? Is it useful?
  • What training have you done recently, and how has it changed your practice?
  • How are physical restraint and consequences used here? Talk me through the last incident you were involved in.
  • What is the home good at, and what could be better?

Principles for answering well

Be honest, including about problems

Inspectors interview a lot of people and detect rehearsed answers quickly. A home where every staff member says everything is fantastic reads as coached, not outstanding. It is entirely acceptable, and often impressive, to say: we struggled with that placement, and here is what we changed. Honesty about weaknesses, paired with evidence that the home learns, is a hallmark of good leadership culture. Never guess or bluff; the strongest professional answer to a question you cannot answer is: I don't know, but I know exactly where I'd find out, followed by where.

Talk about children, not paperwork

Answer with real children (using appropriate confidentiality) and real examples. Compare: we do keywork sessions weekly, with: I do keywork with A on Tuesdays; this month we've been working on travel training because she wants to get to college independently, and last week she did the bus route with me shadowing. The second answer evidences care planning, education support, progress and relationship in two sentences. Specific beats general every time.

Know your safeguarding answers cold

Safeguarding is the one area where hesitation is costly. Every member of staff, including new and agency staff, should be able to state without notes: how to respond to a disclosure (listen, don't promise secrecy, don't ask leading questions, record in the child's words, report immediately); what the missing-from-home procedure is for each child; how to report an allegation against a colleague or manager, including going to the LADO and Ofsted directly if needed; and the home's whistleblowing route. If you cannot answer these today, that is this week's priority, not inspection week's.

Show your working on restraint and consequences

If asked about an incident, describe the build-up, what de-escalation you tried, why any physical intervention was necessary and proportionate, how the child was debriefed, and what changed afterwards. Inspectors are not looking for incident-free homes; they are looking for homes that respond lawfully, reflect and reduce.

It is fine to be nervous

Inspectors expect nerves and generally work hard to put staff at ease. Take your time, ask for a question to be repeated, and do not fill silence with speculation. You are allowed to say that you would like to check a record rather than answer from memory.

What managers should do beforehand

Registered managers should make inspection conversations unremarkable by making their content everyday practice: children discussed by name in every handover and team meeting, supervision that actually explores practice, safeguarding scenarios rehearsed in team meetings, and staff routinely asked the what would you do if questions long before an inspector does. Briefing staff to give particular answers is counterproductive and transparent; briefing staff on what inspection involves, so nobody is ambushed by the format, is simply good support.

Dos and don'ts

Dos

  • Answer with specific, real examples about individual children and their progress.
  • Know your safeguarding, missing and allegations procedures without needing notes.
  • Be honest about difficulties and describe what the home learned and changed.
  • Say I don't know when you don't, and say where you would find the answer.
  • Describe de-escalation and reflection when talking about incidents, not just the incident itself.
  • Know how to contact the LADO and Ofsted directly, and say you would use those routes if needed.
  • Take your time; ask for questions to be repeated.

Don'ts

  • Don't recite rehearsed lines or claim everything is perfect.
  • Don't guess, bluff or speculate to fill silence.
  • Don't talk in paperwork abstractions when a real example is available.
  • Don't minimise incidents or describe consequences and restraint casually.
  • Don't criticise children or share information beyond what the question needs.
  • Don't treat the conversation as an interrogation; inspectors are cross-checking that good practice is real, and if it is, ordinary honesty shows it.
